section_summary: Pages 317–345 continue a translated Japanese technical white paper on industrial recovery, resource use, productivity and economic self-reliance. It compares Japanese technology with developments abroad and argues for research, quality control and better coordination among industries. Three subsequent airgrams report the release of firms from occupation custody, comment on the white paper and announce the easing of industrial commodity allocation controls.

subfiles.title: Translation of Technical White Paper issued by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry
subfiles.from: Ministry of International Trade and Industry
subfiles.about: An assessment of Japanese industrial technology and its role in economic self-reliance.
subfiles.summary: The report urges Japan to improve technology for exports, resource development and living standards. It identifies weak productivity, materials, welding, synthetic products, factory management and coordination among industries, while criticizing dependence on copied foreign methods. It also notes Japanese strengths in adapting technology and calls for greater support for applied research.

subfiles.title: Airgram on release of firms from occupation custody
subfiles.about: Reports that SCAP permitted several formerly vested firms to resume operations in support of Japan's recovery.
subfiles.summary: Reports the release of several firms from occupation custody under continued supervision.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-374 on the Japanese Technical White Paper
subfiles.about: Relays Robert Y. Grant's assessment of the ministry's Technical White Paper.
subfiles.summary: Grant endorses the paper's emphasis on research, technology and resource development, and hopes the ministry will support mining technology agencies.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-375 on lifting allocation controls from industrial commodities
subfiles.about: Reports SCAP's announcement easing allocation controls on industrial commodities from January 1, 1950.
subfiles.summary: Reports planned removal of allocation controls from eighteen commodity categories, including wool, rubber, steel products and selected chemicals.
